column48: Comparison of angiogenin (123 aa) in complex with Fab (this structure) with the structure of free angiogenin [PDB: 1B1I] revealed that antibody binding induces dramatic conformational changes in the cell binding region of angiogenin at the opposite end of the molecule from the antibody binding site. The epitope is located at two loops comprising residues 34-41 and 85-91. Their conformation does not change upon antibody binding. Residues 59-68 comprise the cell binding region. They change their conformation dramatically, Rmsd for ten Calpha atoms is 13.2 Angstrom. In free angiogenin, residues 62-68 are part of a beta-hairpin formed by beta-strands 2 and 3 and the intervening loop 66-68; residues 59-61 lie on a loop that connects the hairpin structure with alpha-helix 3. In the complex, the beta-strand 2 is lost, and the entire 58-67 segment forms a loop that extends much further out from the rest of the molecule than does beta-hairpin. The authors show that antibody binding, not crystal packing, induces the conformational change. The native conformation is critical for the interaction of angiogenin with surface components on its endothelial cell targets. Antibody binding disables angiogenin by destroying the native conformation of the cell binding region.

The structure of the same complex obtained at room temperature [PDB: 2AEQ], for which this paper is a primary citation, is not discussed in the paper. Antigen residues interacting through only water-mediated hydrogen bonds (G196, S245, A246, S247, E276, and (NAG)704B) are not included in the epitope positions, but included in the antigen interacting residues. Antibody residues H: T56, G98, D96; L: N28, T31, S50 interact with the antigen only through water-mediated hydrogen bonds, but not through direct contacts; therefore, they are not included in the curated paratope residues. The epitope consists of four loops of NA and the carbohydrate attached to Asn200. NA loops 195–202 and 216–231 are in contact with the heavy chain CDR1, CDR2 and CDR3 and light chain CDR3. Surrounding these is the NA loop 243–251, in contact with light chain CDR2, NA loop 146–157, in contact with heavy chain CDR1 and CDR2, and sugars NAG200A (A: (NAG)703A) and MAN200H (L: (MAN)217H), in contact with light chain CDR3.

Docking of the Fab-DIII complex onto the cryo-electron-microscopy-derived pseudo-atomic model of the intact West Nile virus virion [PDB: 1P58, 1K4R] showed that with three envelope glycoproteins in the asymmetric unit, there are three potential Fab-binding environments. However, the DIII epitopes are too tightly clustered at the true five-fold axis to permit E16 engagement without steric overlap with adjacent DII residues. Thus, at saturation no more than 120 Fabs can bind the 180 envelope glycoproteins in the mature virion.

column48: Two VEGF monomers assemble in an anti-parallel fashion and are covalently linked by two disulfide bonds. As a result, two antibody molecules bind to two epitopes, which are located on the two opposite poles of the dimer. Both Fab molecules adopt an extended conformation, which gives the complex a rod-like shape. Also, CDR H2 loop packs against loops L3 and H3. This is a highly unusual and non-canonical conformation (the usual conformation is H2 packing against H1 and FR3). Conformational comparison between G6 Fab/VEGF (this structure), B20-4 Fab/VEGF [PDB: 2FJH] and unliganded G6 [PDB: 2FJF] showed that B20–4 approaches VEGF from a different angle compared with G6. More importantly, there is a significant conformational shift of the G6 CDR H2 loop upon VEGF binding.  Specifically, residues H: G50-Y57; of CDR H2 change their position in the bound form, with the biggest movement occurring in the tip of the loop where the Calpha of residue A53 shifts more than 15 Å.

column48: Comparison of the M1295 (this structure) and H2L6 [PDB: 3L5X] crystal structures indicated no significant conformational changes at the CDRs of VH, or at CDR-L1 or CDR-L2. The critical changes between M1295 and H2L6 are located in CDR-L3. The one-amino-acid deletion pulled Asp92 to occupy the space previously held by Asn-Glu, whereas the flanking residues His91 and Tyr94 stayed in approximately the same positions. These changes allowed for a better interaction with IL-13, enabling Asp92 to form a salt bridge with a key epitope residue, Arg11. This salt bridge does not exist in H2L6 because a potential partner, Glu93, points away from Arg11. Another possible improvement is the hydrogen bond between Asp92 and Ser7 at the N-terminus of IL-13. This new interaction extended the epitope by one residue. As a result, the interface area increased by 20 Å2. Although this is a small increase in surface area (only 3%), it contributes to significant improvement in binding affinity. Therefore, replacement of a weak interaction (Asn92) and a non-interacting residue (Glu93) with one residue (Asp92) that is well suited for interacting with Arg11, as well as the increase in surface area due to a new interaction with Ser7, could explain the increase in binding affinity with respect to H2L6.

column48: Free [PDB: 1J0S] and 125-2H-bound (this structure) IL-18 exhibit large conformational differences. Specifically, ""the short alpha-helix from Thr-70 to Asn-77 does pull inward by ∼7.5 Å, toward the IL-18 core, compared with the NMR structure. This inward motion, which is much larger than the void left by mutation of Cys74 to alanine, occurs on the IL-18 surface away from the 125-2H binding site."" The four loops comprised of residues Ser91–Gly95, Arg140–Lys148, Glu152–Gly158, and Lys176–Arg183 undergo significant rearrangement upon binding to the antibody. ""Surprisingly, a cluster of 10 well ordered water molecules is trapped within a cavity formed by binding of the primary and secondary IL-18 loops to 125-2H. There are seven hydrogen-bonding interactions among these water molecules themselves, 10 additional hydrogen bonds between the water molecules and 125-2H, and 11 more between the water molecules and IL-18. Thus, these water molecules form a well ordered, ice like network."" Comparison of the free and IL-18-bound 125-2H structures reveals no significant conformational changes in 125-2H.

The second sugar of each disaccharide ligand [PDB: 3IJY, 3IKC] extends into a permissive binding groove formed by CDR H2, H3, and L2. The two disaccharide ligands differ by the presence of an O-methyl group at position 7 of the terminal Kdo residue, a substitution which is not known to occur in nature. This methyl group generates hydrophobic interactions at the base of the binding groove with ProH98 and IleH96 residues of CDR H3 and results in an increase in surface contact with the antibody. column48: The VH and VL domains of the bound Fab broadly superposed with the 1G4 TCR Valpha and Vbeta domains [PDB: 2BNQ], respectively, with diagonal binding angles of 69° for the 1G4 TCR (8) and 40° for the Fab 3M4E5 (this structure). Additionally, in both TCR and Fabs, the hydrophobic portion of a large residue (TCR R93alpha and Fab Y98VL) arched over the MW motif and was stabilized through hydrogen bonds to the counterpart CDR3 loop (TCR S93beta and Fab E99VH). The contacts are listed in Table S3; residue A:V152 is listed as H152, which doesn't correspond to the PDB file and which is separated from the Fab at more than 4 Å distance.

column48: In the wild-type antibody [PDB: 1Y0L], the carboxylate side chain of GluH50 is anchored within the active site by hydrogen bond interactions with AsnH58 (2.8 Å) and water molecule S21 (3.0 Å), which is further positioned by ThrH35 and TrpH47. These interactions constrain the GluH50 carboxylate to a conformation that is optimally suited for formation of the bidentate salt bridge with the benzimidazolium hapten. Replacement of the catalytic glutamate with aspartate (in this structure) leads to significant losses in hapten affinity (150-fold) and catalytic activity (30-fold). The conformation of AspH50 itself varies somewhat in each of the four noncrystallographic symmetry-related active sites, suggesting enhanced conformational mobility compared with glutamate in the wild-type antibody. Although the AspH50 carboxylate still contacts the hapten, it does not form the bidentate salt bridge. Instead, AspH50 interacts via its Odelta2 atom with the protonated N3 atom of 4 in a monodentate fashion, with the Odelta2-N3 distance in the mutant complexes increased somewhat (2.7–3.1 Å) compared with the wild-type complexes (2.6–2.7 Å). The other oxygen (Odelta1) of AspH50 forms a hydrogen bond with the AsnH58 side chain as in the parent antibody.

column48: The VH and VL domains of the bound Fab broadly superposed with the 1G4 TCR Valpha and Vbeta domains [PDB: 2BNQ], respectively, with diagonal binding angles of 69° for the 1G4 TCR (8) and 40° for the Fab 3M4E5 (this structure). Like the TCR, the Fabs focused the central hotspot of their binding footprint onto the MW peg with the CDR2 VH, CDR3 VH, and CDR3 VL loops playing similar roles to the equivalent TCR Valpha/Vbeta loops. In particular, TCR CDR3alpha residue Y100 and Fab VH CDR3 residue Y103 made hydrogen bonds to the peptide main chain carbonyl oxygen of M4 and their aromatic tyrosine rings interacted closely with the hydrophobic MW motif. column48: METH has only one charged atom available for hydrogen bonding at physiological pH (∼7.4). The METH molecule sits in a deep pocket and is encased almost completely. In addition, the cationic nitrogen forms a hydrogen bond to HisL89 (in PDB, residue A: H230) (3.1 Å) of the light chain. The orientation of the METH molecule, with the aromatic ring near the entrance and the cationic secondary amine pointing to the bottom of the pocket is consistent with the fact that the hapten (+)METH-P6, used in generating and selecting the original IgG, has a linker between the protein and the aromatic ring of METH in the para-position.

column48: Contacts are provided in Figure 2. Electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions dominate the antibody–antigen interface. Three basic residues from CCL2 (Arg18, Arg24, Lys49) form numerous H-bonds to the antibody. Comparison of the Fab structures in the free state [PDB: 4DN3] and in the complex (this structure) reveals conformational changes that accompany binding to CCL2. ""CDRs H3 and L3, most important for CCL2 recognition, do not change their conformation significantly. In CDR L2, only the Asp51 side chain rotates to form a bidentate salt bridge with Arg18 of CCL2. CDRs L1 and H2 exhibit significant conformational rearrangements with the backbone shifts of 2–3 Å and the side chain shifts of up to 4 Å (Phe55 of CDR H2). Upon binding CCL2, CDRs L1 and H2 move toward the center of the antigen. This may be considered as an induced-fit mechanism, which is not typical for high-affinity antibodies that tend to operate in a key-and-lock mode."" Superposition of the available CCL2 crystal structures [PDB: 1DOK, 3IFD] shows that the backbone conformation of the epitope does not change upon binding to the antibody. However, the side chains of the key basic residues Arg18, Arg24 and Lys49 exhibit significant flexibility, which is not very surprising. A major conformational change in CCL2 occurs in the loop 32–38 located on the opposite side of the molecule. The backbone shift at residue 33 exceeds 4 Å. The shift is likely caused by intermolecular contacts in which this loop is engaged in the crystal.

column48: Structural superpositions of the bound PrPc in the different Fab bound complexes indicate limited conformational variations among them. The purportedly therapeutic antibody fragments ICSM18 Fab [PDB: 2W9E] and POM1 Fab (this structure) both recognize an epitope on or near to helix 1 of huPrPc. The binding epitopes for these two antibodies are non-overlapping but lie in close proximity to one another. The Fab fragment of ICSM18 interacts with huPrPc only through helix 1, and the residues of huPrPc involved in this interaction are in the range 142-153. Although both of the antibody Fab fragments, POM1 Fab and ICSM18 Fab, recognize adjacent huPrPc epitopes, the modes of binding of the prion molecules to the respective cognate antibodies are completely different. The common huPrPc epitope, helix 1, is bound to the Fab fragments of these antibodies in an opposite manner. The Fab fragment of VRQ14 binds to ovPrPc [PDB: 1TPX] in a completely different fashion and has a larger epitope that encompasses the N-terminal residues of helix 3 and the loop joining helix 2 and helix 3. This antibody recognizes a prion epitope that would be accessible in both PrPc and PrPsc. Previous structural studies on the VRQ14 Fab with ovPrPc provides some crucial information on the secondary-structural rearrangement during the pathological conversion of PrPc to PrPsc. Unlike the POM1 Fab-huPrPc complex, in which the POM1 Fab heavy chain is the major interacting partner with huPrPc, the interaction interface is evenly shared by the heavy chain and the light chain in the ICSM18 Fab-huPrPc and VRQ14 Fab-ovPrPc complexes. The nature of the interactions between the prion proteins and their cognate antibodies are quite variable among these prion-antibody complexes. Contacts are provided in Table 3.

column48: ""Comparison of linear diUb bound to the Fab with that of free linear diUb [PDB: 2W9N] reveals that the Fab binds the diUb in a bent conformation. The bent conformation exposes the carboxy-terminal tail of the distal Ub and the linkage allowing the Fab to make extensive contacts with these regions. This is similar to the bent conformation seen for K63-linked diUb bound to the K63-specific Fab [PDB: 3DVN and 3DVG]. Alignment of the distal Ubs of linear and K63-linked diUbs in their Fab binding conformations demonstrates that although the distal Ubs could adopt the same conformation, the orientation of the proximal Ubs will differ due to the unique positions of M1 or K63 of the linkage. column48: The crystal structures of 10G5H6 Fab in both complexed (this structure) and uncomplexed [PDB: 4HWE] states aligned well. Upon D3 binding, only minor conformational changes (<1 Å) were seen in most of the CDRs, with the exception of HCDR3. The most important residues (Asn102 and Trp103) from HCDR3 are involved in six hydrogen bonds and extensive van der Waals contacts in the interface (see below) and undergo an approximate 2 Å shift upon D3 binding. The side chain of Arg60 from the heavy chain undergoes a shift to stabilize the 310 helix at the C-terminus of D3. Another important residue, Tyr92, in LCDR3 undergoes a dramatic side-chain shift to contact Leu293 of D3. Epitope residues in both complexed and uncomplexed [PDB: 3BPO] antigens aligned well except the Calpha of Arg230 shifted 4.5 Å; the biggest shift (5.6 Å for Calpha) seen was for Leu293. Arg230 from the B–C loop forms three salt bridges with Asp56 HCDR2 and a hydrogen bond with Trp34 of HCDR1. Phe233 from strand C of D3 is a key residue and its phenyl group makes extensive van der Waals contact with the side chain of Trp103 (HCDR3) of 10G5H6 Fab heavy chain. Another important residue from strand C is Leu232, which forms a hydrogen bond with Asn102 (H3) of 10G5H6 Fab.

column48: TSY_LeuTK adopts an inward-open conformation as a consequence of large hinge-like movements within the core domain relative to the scaffold domain, and shifts in extracellular loops. The most striking change involves TM1a. Tilted by ~45° from its position in the closed state, it protrudes into the predicted location of the membrane. TM6b, in comparison, is rotated away from the central binding site by only 17°. In contrast to the uncoupled movements of TMs 1a and 6b, TMs 1b and 6a tilt by a similar extent (24° and 21°, respectively) towards the scaffold domain, blocking the extracellular pathway. Superimposition of this inward-open and outward-occluded [PDB: 3TU0] structures using only the scaffold domain resulted in an r.m.s.d. in Calpha positions of 3.0 Å. Helices buttressing TM1 and TM6, namely TM2, TM7, and TM5, also undergo substantial rearrangements but their extracellular and intracellular halves move to significantly different extents. Thus, these helices bend, rather than tilt as rigid bodies, facilitated by either a glycine or proline residue located in their midsections. Movement of TM7 causes EL4 to dip down further into the extracellular vestibule, thus closing off the extracellular solvent pathway. To make room for TM6a, TM11 moves away from the center of the transporter, a direction opposite to that seen in the outward-open state [PDB: 3TT1].

column48: ""The species-specific Thr82 that had been identified as the epitope for SG/19 was in fact deeply inserted into the pocket formed by complementarity-determining region (CDR) loops H1, H2, H3, and L3. Furthermore, SG/19 also interacts with betaA domain residues N151, R154, and R155 using its L2 loop outside the CDR core, anchoring the lower half of the alpha1 helix of betaA domain. Because of this two-sided interaction, the H3 loop is wedged between betaA and hybrid domains and prevents the outward swing of the hybrid domain. This resulted in the closed headpiece conformation with the tucked hybrid domain, similar to the ligand-unbound, low-affinity form of the beta3 integrins. The similarity in the overall conformation can readily be appreciated upon structural superposition of the alpha5beta1 headpiece onto the closed alphavbeta3 [PDB: 3IJE]  and alphaIIbbeta3 [PDB: 3FCS]. The three metal-binding sites found in beta3 integrin were also present in beta1, and we could see strong electron density at all sites, indicating that they were occupied.""

column48: ""When compared to natural ligands and ligand-mimetics, a novel feature of the interaction of Fab 107 with low-affinity CD11bA is that a Ca2+ ion is present at MIDAS, coordinated by seven oxygen atoms forming a pentagonal bipyramid, with five oxygens lying in the equatorial plane and two in the axial (apical) positions. column48: ""R217 binds to a conformational epitope that includes the F2 beta-finger (333–341), and a loop and helix (417–423). These regions include residues that are proposed to directly interact with glycans from GpA and have a demonstrated role in erythrocyte binding. K341, N417 and R422 are proposed glycan binding residues that when mutated, reduce binding to erythrocytes. These residues form part of the interface between R217 and RII, demonstrating R217 engages residues in RII that have a functional role in erythrocyte binding. Antibody binding therefore prevents direct receptor binding by blocking the heavily glycosylated GpA from accessing these binding pockets during tight junction formation. A secondary effect of R217 may be through modulation of RII dimerization as dimerization has been proposed to play a role in GpA engagement. The R217 epitope also encompasses residues (L338, T340, K341, N417) found at the proposed dimer interface. Antibody binding may also prevent two RII molecules from coming in close proximity, preventing the F2 beta-finger from inserting into the corresponding F1 cavity of the opposite anti-parallel monomer. This would lead to ablation of putative RII dimerization around a GpA pair that may be necessary for optimal EBA-175 binding to its receptor Glycophorin A."" In contrast, R218 antibody [PDB: 4K2U] binds to an area far removed from functional receptor binding pockets and/or dimerization interface of RII. Contacts are provided in Table S2.

column48: The D25-bound RSV F structure resembled the prefusion structure of the related parainfluenza virus 5 (PIV5) F glycoprotein, indicating that D25 binding stabilizes RSV F in the prefusion conformation. Comparison with the postfusion RSV F glycoprotein structure [PDB: 3RRT, 3RRR, 3RKI] revealed that regions at the N and C termini of the F1 subunit showed marked conformational changes. The fusion peptide, located at the N terminus of F1, and five secondary-structure elements (alpha2, alpha3, alpha4, and the beta3/beta4 hairpin) rearrange and fuse with the alpha5 helix to form a single extended postfusion helix (alpha5post) of >100 Å in length. At the C terminus of F1, the sole parallel strand (beta22) unravels, allowing the prefusion alpha10 helix to move toward the alpha5post helix. ""Whereas the secondary structure of the D25 epitope remains mostly unchanged in pre- and postfusion conformations, the tertiary structure changes substantially, with helix alpha4 pivoting ~180° relative to strand beta2. This explains the failure of D25 to bind postfusion F and suggests that D25 neutralizes RSV by fixing F in its prefusion conformation. D25 binds the least conserved region on the F glycoprotein. Although F proteins from human RSV A and B subtypes are highly related in sequence (447 of 472 or 94.7% of the amino acids comprising the mature F2/F1 ectodomain are identical), six naturally observed sequence variations are located in the region bound by D25. Similarly, of the 56 amino acids in bovine RSV F that are not identical to the mature ectodomain of human RSV F subtype A, 13 are found in this same region. Thus, the D25 epitope, at the apex of the prefusion RSV F structure, may be under immune pressure and serve as a determinant of subtype-specific immunity.""

column48: The FD-AFD binding interface is >20 Å away from the catalytic center, and the interaction of AFD with FD does not change the conformation of the active site pocket or of the oxyanion hole. In the structure of cynomolgus FD [PDB: 4D9Q], the catalytic triad residues His-57, Asp-102, and Ser-195 are in a catalytically incompetent conformation, with the side chain of His-57 pointing away from the active site and the inhibitory loop (residues 212–218) adopting a non-competent conformation as seen in the structures of free FD. In contrast, the inhibitory loop in human FD is rearranged compared with free FD and adopts a competent conformation similar to the one observed in the complex between C3b, FB, and FD. However, the side chain of His-57 is poorly defined in the electron density and was modeled in two different conformations, only one of which is catalytically competent. These differences in residues of the rather flexible active site underscore the lack of an induced conformation by binding of AFD, and it is apparent that AFD can bind the active as well as the inactive conformation of FD. There are nine residue differences between human and cynomolgus FD, all of which, with one exception, are located in regions that are distant from the AFD-binding interface. Residue 178 is the exception, with the Glu-178 side chain of human FD engaged in a weak hydrogen bond interaction with HC Thr-28. In comparison, Gln-178 of cynomolgus FD is engaged in a hydrogen bond interaction with HC Asn-31. These minor differences likely explain the lower affinity of AFD for cynomolgus FD compared with human FD.

column48: Fab40 uses all six CDR loops to bind to a flat epitope at the periphery of the substrate binding cleft, encompassing the 60-loop and 99-loop. The conformation of the catalytic triad (His-57, Asp-102, and Ser-195) has no significant changes compared with other known structures of HGFA and the substrate subsites S1-S4 are unoccupied. The closest atom of Fab40 is > 15 Å from the active site Ser195 residue, indicating an allosteric mode of inhibition. The key feature of the HGFA/Fab40 complex is a large conformational change in the 99-loop. No other significant changes in the HGFA structure are observed. Contacts are provided in Table S1.

H: W96 residue of the Fab heavy chain that is missed in this structure interacts with the antigen in [PDB: 3K2U]. The structure of the generated Trp96H-deletion mutant Ab40.ΔTrp in complex with HGFA showed that the 99-loop had flipped back to the functionally competent state, consistent with assay results showing that the Ab40.ΔTrp/HGFA complex was enzymatically active. Therefore, the 99-loop movement could be considered as an allosteric switch regulating enzyme activity: the allosteric switch is turned ON upon Ab40 binding locking the 99-loop in the noncompetent conformation, whereas antibody removal or binding of the Ab40.ΔTrp mutant turns the allosteric switch OFF, allowing the 99-loop to adopt the competent conformation. Steric clashes occur  between the 99-loop and Trp96H, Ala97H, and Trp98H in CDR-H3 of Fab40 in the competent state.

column48: The epitope adopts an extended conformation, with its bases buried in the protein and its phosphoribose main chain facing away from the protein surface. The binding site is formed by all six CDRs except CDRs H1 and H2. Antibody residues H: Y100, Y100A; form stacking interactions with DNA bases. Also, L: Y92 forms the 5' end of the binding site, where it contacts T1. Conformational comparison between DNA-1 Fab/dT3 (this structure), unliganded DNA-1 Fab [PDB:1XF4], unliganded DNA-1 Fab [PDB:1XF3] and DNA-1 Fab/dT5 [PDB: 1I8M] showed that when comparing the DNA-1 Fab/dT3 structure with the unliganded Fab structures, there is a conformational ordering of the CDR H3 loop including residues H: Y97, R98, P99, Y100,Y100A;. These residues were disordered in the unliganded structures. The conformation of neighboring residues H: 93–96, 100B–102, is very similar between the bound and free Fab molecules. Also, there a 4 Å movement of the main chain of CDR L3 and a shift of the main chain of residue L: Y92 and ordering of its side chain. column48: ca1698 binds to DHFR in a sideways orientation, using residues from all three CDR regions and framework 2. This binding orientation results in a large (883.7 Å2) binding surface area (BSA), and explains to a large extent the dispersed nature of the predicted ca1698 NMR epitope. Almost one third of the BSA in the [DHFR:ca1698] complex contains residues from the Met20 loop, and another third from helix C and the strand C–helix C loop (Table 4). Notably, the CDR3 of ca1698 extends into the substrate binding pocket. Thus, ca1698 is an active site binder. The occupancy of the substrate binding site by CDR3 would lead to competitive inhibition with respect to DHF. However, a detailed kinetic analysis showed that ca1698 gives rise to mixed linear inhibition kinetics with respect to DHF and not pure competitive inhibition. Contacts are provided in Table 4.

column48: The FD-AFD binding interface is >20 Å away from the catalytic center, and the interaction of AFD with FD does not change the conformation of the active site pocket or of the oxyanion hole. In this structure, the catalytic triad residues His-57, Asp-102, and Ser-195 are in a catalytically incompetent conformation, with the side chain of His-57 pointing away from the active site and the inhibitory loop (residues 212–218) adopting a non-competent conformation as seen in the structures of free FD. In contrast, the inhibitory loop in human FD [PDB: 4D9R] is rearranged compared with free FD and adopts a competent conformation similar to the one observed in the complex between C3b, FB, and FD. There are nine residue differences between human and cynomolgus FD, all of which, with one exception, are located in regions that are distant from the AFD-binding interface. Residue 178 is the exception, with the Glu-178 side chain of human FD engaged in a weak hydrogen bond interaction with HC Thr-28. In comparison, Gln-178 of cynomolgus FD is engaged in a hydrogen bond interaction with HC Asn-31. These minor differences likely explain the lower affinity of AFD for cynomolgus FD compared with human FD.

The homodimers in both liganded (this) and unliganded [PDB: 4K3G] structures assume a 2-fold symmetric antiparallel configuration; each VL contacts the other via an interface composed of identical but 180° rotated VL surfaces. A cavity exists between the VLs in both homodimers in the structure. In the liganded complex (this structure), a single MG resides in the cavity, oriented so that the proximal oxygen atom (O1) of the linker points outward, roughly orthogonal to the homodimer surface. MG and the homodimer share a single C2 symmetry axis through the O1 atom of the dye. The peptide backbones of single liganded and unliganded VLs superpose very closely. Local deviations between liganded and unliganded VL main-chain frameworks are found within the CDR3 loop, which, in the liganded complex, makes extensive contacts with both MG and the other VL, and within a non-CDR loop (residues 39–43) that makes a contact with a neighboring VL dimer in the asymmetric crystal unit. Bound MG and structured waters make contacts with the VL domains that are symmetric at the atom level. VL-to-MG bonds occur as pairs, from corresponding atoms on each VL to corresponding atoms (or a single atom) on MG that are 2-fold symmetric with respect to MG geometry. MG contacts with CDR and framework atoms are exclusively van der Waals. The closest contacts with MG are made by Ser89 and Ser91, located near the base of CDR3. MG methyl carbons become wedged into a slot that is formed by Tyr96 side-chain rotation upon binding of the ligand; these 4 carbons account for about half of the total MG/VL contact area. Eight of nine residues that significantly contact MG also make simultaneous contact with the other VL. Binding of MG increases overall VL/VL contacts significantly, with especially large increases for Tyr32 on CDR1 and Tyr55 on CDR2.

column48: This structure and that of the HuPrP(23−231):Nb484 complex [PDB: 4KML] are identical. The major HuPrP:Nb484 interacting surface includes a discontinuous C-terminal segment (residues 164−185) where the binding is stabilized by several H-bonds, salt-bridges, and aromatic interactions. The extensive contacts observed at the interface between the HuPrP C-terminal domain and Nb484 do not induce substantial local structural changes on this segment. The hydrophobic and aromatic interactions governing the proper folding of the beta 2-alpha2 loop and the alpha2-alpha3 helices are conserved like in other WT HuPrP X-ray and NMR structures. One important structural feature of the HuPrP:Nb484 complex is its significant stabilizing effect on the conformation of the beta2-alpha2 loop region. This segment has been described as structurally flexible in all known HuPrP structures, but it is well-defined and rigid when bound to Nb484. column48: ""The E2 core domain has a globular fold, consisting of mostly beta-strands and random coil with two short alpha-helices, which is consistent with previous spectroscopic studies of eE2. The protein contains two, four-stranded antiparallel beta-sheets (termed sheets A and B), the planes of which are approximately perpendicular to each other. The four strands of the N-terminal beta-sheet (sheet A) are stabilized by two disulphide bonds, between strands 1 and 3 (C7 (510) and C8 (554)) and the N-terminal loop with strand 4 (C5 (496) and C9 (566)). The loop between strands 2 and 3 contains sequences implicated in CD81 binding and is flexible, similar to the N-terminal CD81 binding sites, which were deleted14, 15. After strand 4, the polypeptide continues into a long, disordered loop before forming the first short helix (H1) followed by the second beta-sheet (sheet B). A second short alpha-helix (H2) is located between strands 6 and 7. A disulphide bond (C14 (611) and C16 (648)) between strand 6 and the C-terminal strand 8 further stabilizes the fold. The C-terminal strands (7 and 8) are the longest within the protein with approximately nine amino acids each and encompass the 2A12-binding site. 2A12 does not neutralize HCV infection, indicating that the epitope is either buried within the particle or incapable of preventing entry. The two beta-sheets are held together by (1) two disulphide bonds, connecting the loops before strand 1 and after H2 (C4 (488) with C15 (624)) as well as the loops after strand 4 and before H1 (C10 (571) and C13 (601)), and (2) an extensive hydrophobic core consisting of numerous aromatic residues.""

column48: An important feature of the A17λ structure and the key difference between A17λ and A17κ [PDB: 2XZA] is a large interface between the two variable domains of the Fab molecule, where interactions take place between the CDR loops located close to the A17λ active centre, as well as Tyr-H53 from H-CDR2. They include strong direct interactions between residues of the H-CDR3 loop with L-CDR1 and L-CDR2, between H-CDR2 and L-CDR3, as well as contacts via water molecules and a bound MES molecule. These interactions result in the displacement of these CDR loops, apart from H-CDR2, as follows from their structural alignment with the A17κ structure, and in the formation of a fairly rigid ensemble by the two variable domains, unlike in A17κ, where these domains do not interact directly. In contrast, the H-CDR1 loop and the H-CDR2 loop, which lies farther away from the active center, are well aligned in the two structures. The active centre of A17λ structurally deviates from that of A17κ. The major difference is that the upper part of the A17λ active centre is shifted away from the light chain. This shifting of the L-CDR3 loop, which is mainly caused by the strong interaction between Tyr-H53 and Leu-L96, leads to the displacement of Trp-L92 by about 4 Å, its flipping and rotation. This displacement of L-CDR3, and Trp-L92 in particular, which is probably facilitated by the crystal contacts or the presence of the MES molecule, results in the enlargement of the hydrophobic pocket surface and the formation of a lid above the cavity entrance.

column48: The structure of the non-neutralizing mAb#12-epitope structure was compared to that of neutralizing mAb#8 bound to the same peptide [PDB: 4HZL]. As in the case of mAb#8, the complementarity determining region (CDR) H3 loop of mAb#12 was positioned directly over the two key contact residues, Trp437 and Leu438. Residue Trp437 is stabilized further by a hydrogen bond that forms between its side-chain Nε1 and an acidic residue: Asp99 in mAb#12 or Glu39 in mAb#8. Despite certain resemblances, mAb#12 interacts with epitope II in markedly different ways from mAb#8. The number of residues of epitope II required for mAb#12 binding (i.e., Asn434–Phe442) is four residues fewer than that bound by mAb#8 (Asn430–Phe442). As a result, one of the anchors (Glu431) that was identified in the mAb#8–epitope II structure cannot be established in the mAb#12–epitope II structure. In addition, the N-terminal loop of epitope II is loosely held by CDR1 and CDR2 of the heavy chain of mAb#12. In contrast, this loop is extensively involved in the hydrogen bond network with CDR2 and CDR3 of the heavy chain in mAb#8–epitope II. Moreover, the hydrophobic patch of the C-terminal helix in mAb#12–epitope II is packed against CDR3 of the heavy chain and CDR2 and CDR3 of the light chain, whereas the helix is enwrapped by mAb#8 through all three heavy-chain CDR loops, as well as CDR1 and CDR3 of the light chain.

column48: M12B9 Fab binds to four long loops that connect the 4-helix bundle at the tip of L1, presumably away from the viral membrane, in an orientation that is very similar to that of the antibody 7D11 [PBD: 2I9L]. The L1/7D11 and L1/M12B9 complex structures superimpose closely with a low root-mean-square-deviation (RMSD) over all Calpha atoms (L1: 0.53 Å; HC: 1.00 Å; LC: 1.51 Å), which correlates well with the sequence identity, especially within the CDRs of the heavy chain (CDRs H1 and H2; 83.2% sequence identity) that binds L1, with the exception of H3 residues that are not conserved. In the M12B9-Fab/L1 complex, H3 elicits a few extra VdW contacts compared to L1/7D11. However, the bulk of specific interactions (H-bonds and salt-bridges) are formed by CDRs H1 and H2 in a very similar way as reported for the 7D11 complex, while CDR H3 adopts a similar orientation compared to 7D11 but almost exclusively contacts L1 through non-directed VdW interactions. Despite a relatively high structural homology of the Fab domains, Fv light chains present a relatively low sequence identity (67.6%), consistent with the fact that it barely participates in L1 binding.

The AMG 655 binding site on DR5 consists of 11 residues, forming a nearly contiguous region in the cysteine-rich domain 2.

column48: The overall architectures of the GC1008 scFv:TGFß2 (this structure) and GC1008 scFV:TGFß1 [PDB: 4KV5] structures are nearly identical and agree with the previously published structure of GC1008 Fab in complex with TGFbeta3 [PDB: 3EO1]. In all three crystal structures, two molecules of the antibody bind to each TGFbeta homodimer on opposite faces; the overall complex structures all have a 2-fold rotational symmetry with the center of TGFbeta homodimer being the rotation center of the complex. Both monomer chains of the TGFbeta homodimers, as well as the heavy and light chains of the antibody, comprise the antibody:TGFbeta interface. The heavy chain makes contacts with both TGFbeta monomers of the homodimer, while the light chain contacts only one monomer chain of each TGFbeta homodimer. The heavy chain accounts for the majority of interaction surface in both structures reported here, as well as the previously reported structure of GC1008 Fab with TGFbeta3 [PDB: 3EO1]. The epitope interfaces of GC1008 scFv/GC1008 Fab with TGFbeta overlap significantly in all three structures. Contacts are provided in Figure 2 and Table II.

column48: The bestrophin channel is a pentamer of five BEST1 subunits symmetrically arranged around a central axis. It is roughly barrel-shaped with dimensions of ~70 Å across and ~95 Å high. A single ion pore is located perpendicular to the plane of the membrane, along the channel’s axis of symmetry. On the basis of surface hydrophobicity, the protein extends just beyond the extracellular side of the membrane and protrudes ~55 Å into the cytosol. Five Fab fragments bind with 1:1 stoichiometry to the cytosolic region at a subunit interface and radiate outward. Each subunit crosses the membrane four times, predominately as alpha-helices but also as extended conformations. The secondary structure can be divided into four segments accordingly (segments S1–S4). Each segment contributes to the large intracellular region, which appears to be integral to the channel as a whole rather than a domain separate from it.

column48: The ticagrelor binding to MEDI2452 is similar to that of Fab 72 [PDB: 5ALC] with but with some important differences. The CDRs from both Fabs form a highly concave surface and ticagrelor is inserted deep into the interface between VH and VL domains. This type of binding is commonly observed for small haptens. All CDRs except VL CDR2 are contributing directly to ticagrelor binding and a large portion of VH CDR3 is disordered. The combination of the VL CDR3 mutations Asp92Leu and Ser94Asp breaks a hydrogen bond within the VL CDR3 loop to create a more “relaxed” structure. The new conformation is correlated with a 15° tilt of the pyrimidine ring about the attachment of the cyclopropyl-difluorophenyl substituent. The new position of the pyrimidine ring brings it approximately 0.2 Å closer to VH CDR3 Tyr99 in MEDI2452 compared to Fab 72. Moreover, VL Ile93Tyr introduces a hydrogen bond donor which makes interactions with the VH CDR3 loop thus defining the binding site further.

In the SEB molecule, the 3E2 Fab interaction surface overlaps with the MHC binding site but does not interact with the TCR binding site.

column48: The structures of the two POM2 Fab molecules in the asymmetric unit are quite similar. Of all six CDRs of the POM2 Fab, only the CDR H3 loop makes hydrogen bonded interactions with the OR2 peptide, whereas the CDRs in the light chain make interactions with the OR2 peptide via van der Waals and aromatic contact interactions. The 16 residue OR2 peptide is bound to POM2 Fab in a cleft spanning the interface between the variable domains of the L and H chains of the POM2 Fab. In the electron density map, the OR2 peptide in Mol1 could be traced up to Pro P9, whereas in Mol2, the peptide could only be traced up to Gln P8. Neither of the OR2 peptide chains shows sufficient electron density to unambiguously model the second OR of OR2. The OR2 peptide is bound to the POM2 Fab in an extended conformation with a distance of 16.19 and 14.13 Å between the Pro P1 to Gln P8 residues in Mol1 and Mol2, respectively. Intermolecular interactions are listed in Table 2.

column48: Structural analysis revealed that Nb11 does not directly block the furin cleavage site at Ala-173 but binds the short alpha–helix of the G2 domain. The G2 structure is highly similar to the corresponding domain in the human G1–G3/actin complex structure [PDB: 3FFK] characterized by a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 0.84 Å between the two G2 structures, indicating that Nb11 binding does not induce significant conformational changes in G2. Structural comparison of the G2:Nb11 complex with unbound Nb11 [PDB: 4S11] showed that the mechanism of protection does not involve major conformational changes in Nb11 upon G2 binding. Superimposition of the bound and the unbound forms of Nb11 revealed an RMSD of 0.426 Å for 747 atoms. Contacts are provided in Supplementary Table 2.

A structural overlay with the crystal structure of the free Fab [PDB: 5BVJ] shows that the canakinumab paratope is largely pre-organized with minimal induced-fit changes affecting the CDRs. column48: Overall, the 4C2 paratope involves all six CDRs, interacting extensively with mainly the external subdomain of MERS-RBD. Superimposition of the 4C2/MERS-RBD structure with a previously reported structure of the hCD26/MERS-RBD complex [PDB:  4KR0] revealed that the bound 4C2 and hCD26 converge almost perpendicularly to recognize largely different surface patches in the viral ligand. The other half of the gp41 epitope is from glycan N637, which is 98% conserved in HIV-1 strains and is also recognized by PGT151. The 8ANC195 light-chain CDR2, light-chain framework regions (LFR2 and LFR3) and heavy-chain CDR3 contact this glycan. The gp41 glycan N611, which is 99% conserved, is also near the epitope and may interact with the antibody, although electron density for this glycan was not visible in the crystal structure.

The quasi-3-fold is the point where VP1 and VP2 from the ""leftmost"" biological protomer meet with VP3 from the ""rightmost"" protomer. All five VHH contact footprints on poliovirus cover similar areas, nestled into  the deep cleft of the canyon, a location that is typically inaccessible to conventional antibodies. column48: The complex contains a trimeric RBP domain and three nano-L06 moieties. The N-terminal part of the RBP is not visible in the electron density map, as the model could be built from residue Asp 47 to residue Asn 173. The RBP structure starts with a 12-residue-long N-terminal alpha-helix (residues 49 to 61) followed by a 12-strand beta-barrel, constituting the so-called “head” domain. At the “bottom” of the RBP head monomer, a first antiparallel beta-sheet assembles beta1-beta12-beta3-beta8-beta6 and stacks against strands beta2-beta9. At the “top” of the domain, strands beta11-beta4 face the beta7-beta5-beta10 beta-sheet. Each nanobody interacts with two RBP monomers. The interactions reported by the PISA server are quite different at the three interfaces, as the buried surface area (BSA) values of the nanobodies are 638, 609, and 840 Å ^2 for monomers A, B, and C, respectively. The interaction involves the three CDRs but is dominated by CDR3. On the RBP, most of the contacts of the first nanobody are established with the N-terminal helix, and the remaining interactions involve loops 68 to 71, while the second nanobody interacts with loops 113 to 116 and 139 to 142, all of these loops being localized at the RBP “bottom.” Contacts between the RBP and nano-L06 are provided in Table S1.

column48: The crystal contained two copies of peptide-Fab complexes in the asymmetric unit. Electron densities were clearly visible for all 12 residues of IDH1(Ser) peptide bound to one Fab (molecule 1) in the asymmetric unit, while the C-terminal 2 residues of the peptide bound to the other Fab (molecule 2) were disordered. Nevertheless, the visible 10 residues had the same conformation in the two molecules.The MsMab-1 Fab fragment assumes a typical Fab structure consisting of four immunoglobulin-like beta-sandwich domains, and the ligand peptide is packed into a pocket formed by CDR loops L2, L3, H1, and H3. column48: ""Fab(IDE) mediates extensive intermolecular contacts in crystal packing, resulting in fewer interactions among IDE dimers. Fab(IDE) bound IDE D2 via extensive van der Waal interactions and an extensive network of hydrogen bonds. The “elbow” angle between the variable and constant domains was significantly different between the two Fab(IDE) in the asymmetric unit, corresponding to a 12-Å rigid body displacement of the COM of the constant domains. the authors speculate that the Fab–Fab contacts and the flexibility between the variable and constant domains of Fab(IDE) have enabled IDE to crystallize in two distinct conformations within a single crystal. This further demonstrates that Fab serves as an effective crystallization chaperone to reveal conformational states that are otherwise difficult to crystallize.""

R10 binds to the viral surface along the edges of the pentameric building block of the virus, between the twofold and threefold axes. Tight binding is facilitated by 19 hydrogen bonds, the antibody components of these include the side-chain of Y48 (L-chain), and main-chain carbonyl groups of V103 (H-chain) and L53 (L-chain), which interact with K150 (VP3) and R209 (VP3), respectively, and indirectly with R67 (VP2). Thus, the mutations mainly result in different charge distributions on the light-chain surface. In mutant 5, the R29A(L) and Y32A(L) mutations produce a slight shift in the main-chain for FRL2 (residues 48, 49), CDRL2 (50–56), FRL3 (57–72) and CDRL1 (24–32) with maximum Calpha differences observed in CDRL2 (1.3 Å for Lys51(L)), FRL3 (0.9 Å for Gly68(L)) and CDRL1 (0.9 Å between Arg29(L) and Ala29(L); S4 Fig). The shift for CDRL2 in mutant 5 may be the direct result of substituting Tyr32(L) with alanine, which allows the nearby Phe48(L) side chain to rotate and influence the conformation of Lys51(L), Asn52(L) and Asn53(L). None of the mutations affect binding to T117v2, as the mutant CDRH3 conformations are almost identical to wild-type 10E8. In mutant 5, where R29(L) and Y32 (L) are mutated to alanine, glycerol (used for cryoprotection) is not observed at the lipid-binding site in either of the two Fabs in the asymmetric unit, suggesting that the lipid binding site is severely disrupted by these mutations.

The H3 loop of S4 approaches the matriptase S1 pocket at the active site in a way that extends residue ArgH100b into the binding pocket and presents the putative scissile bond in a reverse orientation.

column48: The inhibitor A11 Fab binds to matriptase and caps the active site through numerous interactions with the protease surface loops. Furthermore, binding of the antibody to matriptase did not result in remote conformational changes at either the oxyanion hole or the activating Val16–Asp194 salt bridge. The heavy-chain loops of A11 make contacts with the 60s and 90s loops of matriptase while the H3 loop of A11 forms a beta-hairpin turn that reaches into the substrate-binding pocket of the active site but makes few contacts with the protease. The A11 light-chain complementarity-determining region 3 loop binds in a groove between the 90s and 170s loop on the protease. The light-chain complementarity-determining region 1 loop also makes several contacts with the protease 170s and 220s loops.

The different Fabs were bound to recently defined elements of the V3 crown: the “arch” at the tip (beta-turn) of the V3 loop (P312–P315), the “circlet” composed of regions in the N- and C-terminal beta-strands of the crown (P306–P309 and P316–P317), and the “‘band” at the N- and C-terminal ends of the V3 crown (P304–P305 and P318). For the VH5-51 mAbs, the arch containing the GPGR/Q motif plays a minor role in binding. Instead, there are two clusters of residues, with the largest contact area in the circlet and band regions of the V3 crown that are common contact sites for all five VH5-51 derived Abs: i) R/KP304, KP305 and YP318 in the band and ii) IP307, R/H/AP308, IP309 F/LP317 in the circlet. Interestingly, at three positions, (P304, P308 and P317), the residues were different in the three V3 peptides in complex with the various Fabs, but the contact area in Å^2 was similar, confirming the tolerance of anti-V3 mAbs for variation at these positions.

column48: The crystallographic asymmetric unit contained 3 copies of TNFalpha-certolizumab Fab complex with a non-crystallographic 3-fold symmetry. When viewed along the 3-fold axis, the trimeric complex had a shape that resembles a three-bladed propeller, with one protomer representing one blade. It consisted of three certolizumab Fab fragments radially bound to a single TNFalpha homotrimer. Superimposing TNFalpha in the TNFalpha-certolizumab Fab complex with its receptor-bound form [PDB: 3ALQ] indicated no significant overall structural changes, except for the conformational change of the DE loop region due to the interaction with certolizumab. The elbow angle of the certolizumab Fab fragment, defined as the angle subtended by the two pseudo-dyad axes relating the variable and constant domains of the Fab fragment, did not differ between the TNFalpha-bound and the free certolizumab [PDB: 5WUV], despite the intrinsic flexibility of the Fab elbow. Additionally, all CDRs of the structure of the uncomplexed certolizumab Fab fragment had the same conformation as those of this antibody in complex with TNFalpha, implying that this antibody drug maintains the CDRs in productive binding conformations prior to interactions with TNFalpha.

column48: The overall conformation of the antibody and the conformations of the CDRs were similar in the uncomplexed [PDB: 3RVT, 3RVU] and complexed crystal forms [PDB: 3RVV, 3RVW, 3RVX], suggesting that CDRs of mAb 4C1 do not undergo significant rearrangements upon allergen binding. From the allergens, the most important residues for interaction were Arg18, Ser19(Gln in Der p 1), Arg21, Arg157, Gln182, Tyr186, and Asp199. Superimposition of the Der f 1, Der p 1, Der f 1-4C1 [PDB: 3RVV], and Der p 1-4C1 [PDB: 3RVW, 3RVX] structures showed that the antigen residues Asp16, Arg18, Ile159, Tyr186, Asp199, Tyr202, and Tyr204 had very similar conformations in all these structures. They formed a central “rigid” surface to which the antibody binds, and Arg157 worked as an anchor to form additional interactions that stabilize the complex. Residue Arg157 participated in several H-bonds and interacted with each CDR from the light chain. The mAb 4C1 binding epitopes on Der f 1 and Der p 1 were very similar but have some distinct features. The largest conformational differences between uncomplexed and complexed allergens were observed within Der p 1 where antibody binding caused changes that affected the region formed by residues 181–183. Residue 181 differs in Der f 1 (Thr) and Der p 1 (Ala). After complex formation, Thr181 present in Der f 1 formed a hydrogen bond with Glu106 from the heavy chain of the antibody. In Der p 1, formation of the H-bond was impossible, and the alanine was pushed away from the antibody Glu106. The change in the alanine position was propagated to Gln182, which shifted ∼3 Å (Calpha position) and significantly changed its side chain conformation.

column48: Nanobody VHH#1 associates with the trimeric TNF to form a hetero-hexameric TNF-Nanobody complex. VHH#1 attaches to the concave surface of the outer beta-sheet of TNF and contacts two TNF monomers simultaneously. VHH#1 covers 1,246 Å^2 of the TNF solvent-accessible surface area, of which 902 Å^2 belongs to one TNF monomer and 274 Å^2 to the other monomer. Its three CDRs interact with TNF, but CDR2 and especially CDR3 are predominant in the interaction, as commonly observed in other Nanobody complexes. VHH#1 is aligned almost parallel to the TNF surface (when comparing the orientations of their beta-strands), and its CDR2 lines the TNF surface.

column48: The Fab 6649 engages an epitope on the side of the HA1 head domain. It approaches HA with its long axis normal to the trimer threefold axis and contacts the head with both heavy and the light chains. CDRs L1 and L3 bind a conserved loop (residues 125–128; H3 numbering, used here throughout), while CDRH3 and framework residues of the heavy chain contact the edge of beta5, the strand farthest from the trimer threefold axis. The antigen-combining site includes 12 hydrogen bonds, six with main-chain carbonyls or amides on HA. Sequences of HAs from H1N1 influenza viruses circulating from 1977 to 2009 and mapped onto the HA structure show that the Fab6649 epitope was conserved during that entire period.

A superimposition of MERS-4 Fab with MERS-4V2 scFv revealed that their respective recognition was largely mediated through interactions with the beta5-beta6, beta6-beta7, and beta7-beta8 loops in the receptor-binding subdomain of the RBD. column48: Eleven copies of the crystal structure of Fab311-(NPNA)3 could be fit into the EM map. The repeat region of rsCSP is well defined with continuous cryo-EM density and forms an unusual extended spiral structure, from which multiple Fab311 antibodies radiate tangentially in a pseudo-helical arrangement. In the cryo-EM map, however, two additional Fabs were observed, demonstrating that 11 Fabs can bind simultaneously to rsCSP, although the density for the N- and C-terminal Fabs was sparse. In addition, no density was observed for the N-terminal or C-terminal alphaTSR domains of rsCSP, likely due to flexibility. The cryo-EM structure determines unambiguously that the epitope consists of only two NPNA repeats. The Fabs are so closely packed against one another that their two epitopes are seamlessly stitched together without the need of an additional repeat as a spacer. Fabs are positioned such that the groove in which the peptide resides extends from one Fab directly into the other. The two repeats of the NPNA epitope adopt a type I beta-turn followed by a pseudo 3(10) turn that repeats throughout the length of the spiral structure. Furthermore, we observed that Fab311 is able to bind the NVDP repeats, thereby increasing the available epitopes on rsCSP from 15 (NPNA only) to 22 (including the DPNA and NPNV repeats).

column48: The epitope of 21c has been structurally characterized as including both a foreign antigen (gp120; chain F) and a self-antigen (CD4; chain G). column48: Each RNA molecule in the Fab–RNA complex makes crystal contacts with its three neighboring RNA molecules. Overall, dV RNA from HAV IRES folds into a Y-shaped structure that consists of two helical stems, P2 and P3 closed by loops L2 and L3, respectively, bifurcated from a base helical stem, P1, formed by base pairing between the 5′- and 3′-ends. These three helical stems, P1, P2, and P3, form a three-way junction where the P2 and P3 helices stack coaxially. The P1 helix protrudes from the P2-P3 helical axis towards the P2 helix with no unpaired nucleotides between P1 and P3. An unpaired region within the P1 helix, L1, forms an asymmetric bulge between the P1a and P1b helical stems. This bulge strongly kinks the RNA backbone, bending helix P1a toward helix P3. The L1 motif constitutes the binding site for Fab HAVx.

column48: The final RSV F-R4.C6 structural model has a RSV F trimer surrounded by the Fv domains of three R4.C6 Fab molecules. The central RSV F has three protomers with each protomer composed of F2 and F1 that are covalently linked by two disulfide bonds. The N- and C-terminal domains of F1 in each protomer pack together to form a six-helical bundle, a key characteristic shared by many membrane-fusion proteins in post-fusion state. Each R4.C6 recognizes a quaternary epitope on RSV F that consists of antigenic site II on one protomer, and antigenic site IV on another protomer. Four complementarity determining regions (CDRs) of R4.C6 are involved in interacting with RSV F. The heavy chain HCDR2 and HCDR3 and light chain LCDR1 and LCDR2 of R4.C6 interact with antigenic site II. The R4.C6 LCDR2 and HCDR3 are in close contact with RSV F antigenic site IV spanning residues 422–471 on a neighboring protomer.

column48: Each of the three gp120–gp41 protomers exhibited outwardly rotated gp120 subunits compared to closed Env trimers, a largely disordered and exposed V3 loop, a displaced V1V2 region and a four-stranded gp120 bridging sheet. The E51 Fab epitope on gp120 overlaps with the epitopes for the CD4i antibodies 17b and 21c. Consistent with mass spectrometric identification of sulfated tyrosines in E51 Fab, density for two sulfated tyrosines within the E51 CDRH3 was observed. While Tys100I(E51 HC) showed clear density for both the aromatic ring and sulfate group, the density for Tys100F(E51 HC) was weaker. The E51 epitope on gp120 involves the base of V3 and residues within the four-stranded beta20–beta21–beta2–beta3 bridging sheet and E51 also contacts the CD4-binding site loop . E51 Fab contacts gp120 with all three CDRs of its heavy chain, but its light chain does not participate in gp120 recognition. Contacts between the E51 heavy chain and gp120 could be divided into two categories: (1) CDRH1 and CDRH2 contacts with gp120 bridging sheet residues and CDRH3 stacking on top of the bridging sheet and (2) interactions between CDRH3 sulfotyrosines and positively charged gp120 residues.

column48: The structure of MBG bound to the Fab fragment of KoH body H4H14401P showed that the arrangement of the variable domains of this KoH Fab is very similar to that seen in Bence-Jones proteins. The KoH Fab has a deep pocket at the center of the CDR surface, like most Bence-Jones proteins, and 1 molecule of MBG is bound in this pocket. The MBG is contacted by a set of tyrosines and tryptophans from CDRs L1, L3, KoH2, and KoH3. Although this Fab has a long CDR1 in its VKoH, this CDR, encoded by the IGKV4-1 gene, does not contact the MBG. The other 5 CDRs adopt conformations close to those of conventional antibody light chains with similar sequences. In addition to the primary bound MBG molecule, a second MBG molecule sits nearby, making a crystal contact between the CDR surface of one KoH Fab and the CK domain of a second KoH Fab. The authors conclude that the second MBG molecule is most likely a crystal packing artifact.

All complementarity-determining region (CDR) loops contribute to the binding groove with the heavy and light chains providing roughly an equal proportion of the total buried surface area.

column48: The monoclinic crystal of 3.3-Fab/PEG complex contains four Fab fragments in an asymmetric unit, with heavy chains (named H, I, J, K) and light chains (L, M, N, O). It binds to the N-terminal side of the Fab, which corresponds to the complementarity determining regions (CDRs), in a symmetrical way. In addition to the central S-shaped core fragment of PEG, there is a smaller satellite PEG fragment on each side of the core. The sizes of the modeled PEG fragments are significantly smaller than those used in crystallization and they might belong to a single PEG molecule. The flexible regions between them were exposed to solvent and thus not visible. The three central ethylene glycol units of the S-shaped PEG fits into a cleft at the Fab-Fab interface.

column48: The crystal structure of compound 14 bound to the PCSK9ΔP′–Fab7G7 complex was determined  and provided the molecular details of the antagonistic activity. The herein used “open groove” form PCSK9ΔP′ lacks the P′ helix to facilitate the groove interaction of the compound, whereas the crystallization chaperone Fab7G7 was critical to opening up access of the compound to both the groove and the EGF(A) binding sites in the crystal lattice. The Fab7G7 epitope is on module 2 (M2) of the PCSK9 C-terminal domain. Binding of Fab7G7 induced some local conformational changes in M2, involving the two antiparallel beta-strands 2 and 5. On the other hand, Fab7G7 stabilized the T573–Q584 region, which in all reported PCSK9 structures is fully or partially disordered.

column48: The interaction between the Fab and the receptor is primarily mediated by the CDR loops of each antibody chain. The epitope on IL-36R is on a side of the molecule remote from the expected IL-36 ligand/antagonist binding site. The majority of the buried surface on IL-36R is contributed by D2 and the D1-D2 linker; only one residue in D1, Trp87, appears to contribute significantly to the interface. On both the VH and VL chains of the Fab, all three CDR loops interact with IL-36R. While the majority of the VL chain interactions are confined to the D1-D2 linker, the VH chain interacts extensively with both D2 and the D1-D2 linker.

column48: P46 presents the topology of the periplasmic binding proteins (PBP) superfamily consisting of two similar alpha/ß globular domains connected by a three-stranded hinge. The four P46–FabP46 complexes found in the asymmetric unit are organized as a pair of two complexes related by twofold noncrystallographic symmetry. Each P46 subunit shows extensive inter-actions with two FabP46 subunits. However, only one of these two FabP46 subunits presents a consistent paratope interacting with P46 through the CDRs. All light- and heavy-chain CDRs, with the exception of LCDR2, interact directly with P46 by a network of hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonds. The corresponding epitope in P46 exclusively includes residues from the C-domain. Overall, the structural epitope in P46 comprises 12 residues, ﬁve interacting with the FabP46 light chain (VL) and seven interacting with the heavy chain (VH). Comparison of unbound FabP46 [PDB: 6RNN] and of FabP46 in the complex showed that the CDRs experience only very small rearrangements upon binding to P46.

The Fab contacts glycopeptide with CDR’s L3, H1’, H2’, and H3’, with some contributions from heavy-chain framework residues; the largest contribution comes from CDR H2’.

The structured C-terminal domain (residues 125–225) of PrP comprises three alpha-helices (alpha1–alpha3) and a short, two-stranded, anti-parallel beta-sheet. Residue 127 immediately precedes the ﬁrst beta-strand of the beta-sheet whereas residue 129 lies within it. The residues surrounding 127 and 129 are well deﬁned in the crystal structure and show that the side-chains of both residues are predominantly located on the protein surface.
